extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (epistemology/empiricism); general readers of Locke
extracted.subtask_description: Analyse and explain John Locke's account of simple ideas, the distinction between primary and secondary qualities, and his theory of perception as given in these chapters. Focus on origins of ideas, how bodies produce ideas, and how judgment/habit shapes perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: All simple ideas the mind has are received only by the two ways of sensation and reflection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke asserts that whatever simple idea we have must be derived from either external sensation or internal reflection; readers are asked to 'assign any SIMPLE IDEA which is not received from one of those inlets' to test this claim. Examples: ideas of number, extension, etc., are traced to these two sources; the text compares combinatorial power of letters to show how limited simple elements can produce vast complex thoughts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and Unity as basic simple ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Existence and Unity are among the simple ideas suggested by external objects and internal ideas; whatever we can consider as one thing suggests unity, and objects suggest existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are named as fundamental simple ideas alongside others; Locke treats them as immediately suggested by experience (externally and internally) without further decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Power
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of power is a simple idea arising from observing our own ability to will/move and the effects bodies produce upon one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke uses inner observation (we can move parts of our bodies) and external observation (bodies producing effects) to justify power as a simple idea; this provides an account for how we conceive causal capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idea of Succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Succession is a simple idea suggested chiefly by the continual passing in train of ideas in our minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke points to introspection of the mind's sequence of ideas (one going and another coming) to derive the notion of succession; this supports his claim that some ideas originate primarily from reflection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are the materials of all knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas are made out of simple ideas; the few simple ideas suffice to constitute all other knowledge and fancy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that just as many words derive from few letters, the mind combines simple ideas (e.g., number, extension) to compose complex ideas. Readers should treat claims to innate ideas skeptically in light of this combinatorial account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive ideas may arise from privative causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when the external cause is a privation (an absence), the mind can form a clear, positive idea (e.g., darkness or shadow produces the idea of darkness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that impressions produced by absence (privations) can still be perceived as positive ideas; he gives shadow as example and notes painters/dyers have clear ideas of colours without causal knowledge. He considers physiological explanations (changes in animal spirits) but leaves full determination open.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: ideas in the mind vs qualities in things
rubrics_metrics.description: We must distinguish ideas (immediate objects of perception in the mind) from qualities in external objects that produce them; investigating causes belongs to inquiry into external things, not to the idea itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke repeatedly warns against conflating the idea with the external cause: e.g., perceiving whiteness is distinct from analyzing the particles that produce whiteness. This distinction underpins later divisions of qualities and deflates naive realism about secondary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary qualities are real and resemble our ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary/original qualities (solidity, extension, motion or rest, number or figure) are wholly inseparable from bodies and truly exist in them; ideas of these qualities are resemblances of the qualities themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues these qualities persist under division and are present in every particle; they are 'real' because they exist in bodies whether observed or not. He offers the grain-of-wheat division thought experiment and notes geometric/mathematical richness (extension) to illustrate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities are powers to produce ideas and do not resemble those ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities (colour, taste, smell, sound, heat) are not in the objects as our ideas represent them but are powers—depending on primary qualities—to produce sensations in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke explains that colours and tastes depend on the bulk, figure, texture, and motion of insensible parts; these ideas have no resemblance in the objects. Examples: flame produces idea of heat and light, snow produces white and cold; porphyry appears coloured only in presence of light. Secondary qualities are effects of particles acting on our organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: How bodies produce ideas: impulse and motion in organism
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodies produce ideas by impulse—motion transmitted (via nerves/animal spirits) to the seat of sensation (brain)—and not by being united to the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke asserts physical contact and motion are the only conceivable ways bodies act on one another; he hypothesizes imperceptible particles convey motion to sensory organs. This mechanical account undergirds his explanation of both primary and secondary qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold classification of qualities in bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities in bodies rightly considered are of three sorts: (1) primary qualities (bulk, figure, number, situation, motion/rest); (2) powers to produce ideas immediately (sensible/secondary qualities); (3) powers to change other bodies so they produce different ideas (mediate secondary powers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke enumerates and distinguishes these three sorts and explains their relations: the first are 'real' in the things, the second are commonly (but mistakenly) thought real, and the third are acknowledged as mere powers; examples include sun whitening wax (third sort) vs producing ideas of light/heat (second sort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary qualities: immediate vs mediate perceivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary qualities are twofold: those immediately perceivable (operate directly on our bodies to produce ideas) and those mediately perceivable (operate on other bodies, altering them so they produce ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke closes the chapter by distinguishing qualities that affect our senses directly (colours, tastes) from those that act via change in other bodies (sun bleaching wax). This nuance refines classification and causal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as the first simple idea of reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception (or thinking in general) is the first simple idea gained by reflection; bare perception is mostly passive, whereas thinking (in the English sense) implies active, voluntary attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke invites readers to introspect to recognize perception, emphasizing that reflection (not discourse) gives the idea. He contrasts passive perception (cannot avoid perceiving) with active thought (voluntary attention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception requires notice in the understanding (impulse on organ insufficient)
rubrics_metrics.description: A merely sufficient physical impulse on a sensory organ does not constitute perception unless the motion reaches the understanding and is taken notice of; hence sensation depends on the mind's taking notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke gives examples: while intently contemplating, one may not perceive sounds though the ear is physically stimulated; fire may burn without perception if the motion doesn't reach the brain. This principle separates physiological stimulus from conscious perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment and habit modify sensations into perceived ideas (unnoticed changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: In grown persons, sensations are often unconsciously altered by judgment and habit into 'perceptions' that attribute causes (e.g., sight's habitual inference of convexity from shadow), so that what is really sensation is taken as perception of external cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke illustrates with the blind-then-seeing thought experiment (cube vs sphere) and with how sight habitually translates plane coloured patches into ideas of convex bodies. He emphasizes rapid, habitual mental operations that convert raw sensations into judged perceptions without conscious awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as a distinguishing mark of animals
rubrics_metrics.description: The faculty of perception distinguishes animals from plants; perception exists in some degree in all animals, adapted to their state and needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues that although some plants show motion, it is mechanistic and not sensation; perception varies in degree across animals. This provides a biological/teleological implication of his account of perception.
